The '''relativistic propagation equation of [[light]]''' models the trajectory of [[photon]]s on [[the cosmological scale]]:

$$
c^2dt^2
=
a^2(t)\left[
\frac{dr^2}{1-kr^2}
+
r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)
\right]. \tag{1}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q2580}}</ref>

== Derivation ==

{{Hidden proof}}
Let $l$ denote length, $t$ time, and $c$ the speed of light.

On local scale, Newtonian mechanics is valid, hence

$$
dl=cdt
$$

By the [[comoving coordinates#Metric_function|defining metric function]] of comoving coordinates,

{{#content:Q2604|noNote}}

Hence 1.
{{End hidden}}

== Special case: Along radial trajectory ==

Choosing [[comoving coordinates]] s.t. the $\theta,\phi$ coordinates of the [[photon]] stay constant ($d\theta,d\phi=0$), then

$$
\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-kr^2}}
=
\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\frac{c}{a(t)}\,dt. \tag{2}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q2580}}</ref>

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
\because d\theta,d\phi=0 \\
\therefore r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)=0 \\
\therefore c^2dt^2 = a^2(t) \frac{dr^2}{1-kr^2}
\therefore cdt = a(t) \frac{dr}{\sqrt{1-kr^2}},
$$

hence 2.

{{End hidden}}
